**Proposed mechanism:** AP4B1 (HGNC:24140) —DISRUPTS→ AP-4 dependent protein transport (GO:0007057); AP-4 dependent protein transport (GO:0007057) —LEADS_TO→ Intellectual disability (HP:0001249); DNM2 (HGNC:2777) —DISRUPTS→ Endosomal trafficking and membrane remodeling (GO:0007057); BIN1 (HGNC:1101) —DISRUPTS→ Endosomal trafficking and membrane remodeling (GO:0007057); Endosomal trafficking and membrane remodeling (GO:0007057) —LEADS_TO→ Centronuclear myopathy (HP:0003174). While AP-4-dependent intellectual disability results from haploinsufficiency in AP4B1 affecting AP-4 dependent transport, centronuclear myopathy arises from gain-of-function mutations in DNM2 and BIN1, both critical regulators of endosomal trafficking and membrane remodeling. The convergence lies in the shared pathway of endosomal trafficking and vesicle-mediated transport, which, when disrupted by different mechanisms (haploinsufficiency vs. dominant gain-of-function), leads to distinct but related cellular dysfunctions manifesting as the respective phenotypes.

**How to falsify it:** Demonstration that mutations in BIN1 or DNM2 do not impair endosomal trafficking or membrane remodeling, or that AP4B1 mutations do not affect AP-4 dependent transport, would falsify this hypothesis. Furthermore, if genetic studies reveal no overlap in affected cellular pathways between patients with AP-4-dependent intellectual disability and those with centronuclear myopathy, this link would be refuted. _(variant: Discovery of common, benign variants in the coding regions of BIN1 or DNM2 in the general population (gnomAD frequency > 1%) that do not segregate with centronuclear myopathy would weaken the claim of dominant gain-of-function mutations.)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding this mechanistic link could reveal novel therapeutic targets for both diseases. For instance, strategies to modulate endosomal trafficking or cytoskeletal dynamics might be beneficial for both conditions, even if initiated by different genetic defects. This highlights the potential for cross-disease therapeutic development by targeting common downstream pathways.
